notes.text: Everything a customer says twice gets written down. Reviewed monthly, and it is the least glamorous, most useful document we keep. Recurring themes, ranked by frequency Noise at peak. The room is hard-surfaced and loud from 7:30 to 9. Third most common complaint and the one we have done least about. The queue at 8am. Addressed partly with the double points hour in Loyalty Program to shift demand earlier. Single Origin Ethiopia Guji as espresso. Roughly one in four sends it back. This produced the standing rule to offer a taste first, now in Barista Training Plan. Wanting oat milk at no upcharge. We hold the upcharge, per Pricing Strategy. Not enough seating with power outlets for the afternoon laptop crowd. Two spikes worth remembering. Three weeks of complaints after the 11% price increase in year two. Two weeks of complaints about the blend tasting wrong during a Colombia stockout, traceable to Green Bean Inventory and to improvising House Blend Ember instead of telling people. Praise clusters almost entirely on staff by name, which is the strongest argument for the investment in Barista Training Plan and the retention approach in Payroll and Tips Policy. Themes here feed Seasonal Menu Autumn decisions and the churn reasons in Subscription Churn Notes. Related: Regulars and Community, Espresso Machine Maintenance

notes.label: Regulars and Community
notes.excerpt: About 180 people account for a little over half of café revenue. They come in three to six times a week and they are the business. Who they are. The 6:30 crowd, mostly trades and hospital shifts, drip and a morning bun, in and out in four minutes. The 8am commuters, milk drinks, the queue noted in Customer Feedback Log. The 10am freelancers, who stay two hours and want an outlet. The Saturday families, who buy bags and ask about the Farmers Market Booth. What keeps them. Their name, their order remembered, and the same face behind the bar — which makes staff turnover the single biggest risk to this group and the reason for Payroll and Tips Policy and Barista Training Plan. Community things we do and will keep doing: a free monthly public cupping, promoted only in Email Newsletter Strategy; the community board by the door; hosting the neighbourhood association for the price of a carafe; the high school jazz trio in December. These are the people who make Second Location Analysis a hard question — they belong to this room, not to the brand. Related: Regulars and Community, Seasonal Menu Autumn, Local Press Outreach

notes.label: Subscription Churn Notes
notes.excerpt: 410 active subscribers. 12oz or 2lb, every two or four weeks, shipped or collected. About $7,100 a month combined with retail bags in Monthly PnL Summary. Monthly churn is 6.5%, which means we replace half the book every year. Exit reasons, from cancellation replies: "Too much coffee" — 34%. The single biggest cause and entirely a cadence problem, not a product problem. Offering a four week interval before cancelling saves about a third of these. "Too expensive" — 21%. Mostly shipping, not coffee, which is a packaging and rate question for Supplier Directory. "Wanted variety" — 18%. Monthly churn is 6.5%, which means we replace half the book every year. Exit reasons, from cancellation replies: "Too much coffee" — 34%. The single biggest cause and entirely a cadence problem, not a product problem. Offering a four week interval before cancelling saves about a third of these. "Too expensive" — 21%. Mostly shipping, not coffee, which is a packaging and rate question for Supplier Directory. "Wanted variety" — 18%. Rotating single origins for anyone who has taken three shipments. Collection in store instead of shipping, which also drives a café visit and a pastry from Pastry Partnership. Subscribers are disproportionately drawn from Loyalty Program members at fifty drinks, and from the conversations at the Farmers Market Booth. Related: Customer Feedback Log, Quarterly OKRs, Cost of Goods Breakdown

notes.text: Seven accounts, $12,600 a month, roughly 21% of revenue and the most stable line in Monthly PnL Summary. The book Ledger & Loom (bookshop café) — 18kg a week of House Blend Ember, our largest and oldest account, found us at the Farmers Market Booth. Third Rail Diner — 12kg a week, blend only, price sensitive, never complains. Hartwell Hotel — 9kg a week plus a decaf line, the account that demanded consistency and taught us to log every batch in the Roasting Schedule. Two office contracts, 6kg a week combined, low touch, high margin. Two small cafés at 4kg each, both of which came from the coverage in Local Press Outreach. How it works. Roasted Tuesday, delivered Wednesday morning, net 15. Price ladder by volume, held in Pricing Strategy. Margin runs 52-58% cost per Cost of Goods Breakdown, thinner than retail but with no labour attached beyond delivery. What loses an account: inconsistency, not price. Two accounts churned in year two, both after we improvised the blend during a Colombia stockout — the exact failure recorded in Green Bean Inventory. Partners get a quarterly note on upcoming lots and price changes, kept separate from the consumer list in Email Newsletter Strategy. The canned cold brew from Cold Brew Recipe is the obvious next product for this channel. Related: Equipment Loan Terms, Second Location Analysis, Quarterly OKRs

See Cold Brew Recipe. Retail bags: 42-46%. Thin, but it buys at-home habit and feeds the subscription tracked in Subscription Churn Notes. notes.label: Equipment Loan Terms
notes.excerpt: Two financed assets, both on the books, both nearly paid down. La Marzocco Linea PB, bought used in year one for $14,500. Five year note at 7.9%, $293 a month, 14 payments remaining. This is the machine whose care is documented in Espresso Machine Maintenance and whose failure closes the café. Loring 12kg roaster, bought in year two for $52,000 with a $12,000 deposit. Seven year equipment note at 6.4%, $947 a month, 41 payments remaining. It is the asset that made Wholesale Accounts possible and it sets the ceiling on how much we can roast per week under the Roasting Schedule. Combined $1,240 a month, carried as a line in Monthly PnL Summary. Terms worth remembering. No prepayment penalty…

The roaster is insured for replacement value, the espresso machine for depreciated value, which is a mistake we should fix at renewal. Capacity note: the Loring runs about 96kg of green a week across two roast days before we would need a third, which is the constraint behind the growth targets in Quarterly OKRs. Related: Cost of Goods Breakdown, Supplier Directory

Any expansion case, including Second Location Analysis, starts from this page and the targets in Quarterly OKRs. Related: Pricing Strategy, Green Bean Inventory

notes.label: Pricing Strategy
notes.excerpt: We are the second most expensive coffee within a mile and intend to stay there. Cheapest is a race we lose on volume; most expensive invites a comparison we cannot always win. Second is comfortable — the positioning mapped in Competitor Landscape. Current prices: drip $3.50, cortado $4.25, latte $5.25, pourover $6.00, cold brew $5.50, 12oz House Blend Ember $18, 12oz Single Origin Ethiopia Guji $22. Principles we hold to: Raise prices annually by a small amount rather than rarely by a large one. A 4% increase produced no measurable complaint; the 11% jump in year two produced three weeks of them in Customer Feedback Log. Never discount the coffee. Reward frequency instead through Loyalty…
notes.text: We are the second most expensive coffee within a mile and intend to stay there. Cheapest is a race we lose on volume; most expensive invites a comparison we cannot always win. Second is comfortable — the positioning mapped in Competitor Landscape. Current prices: drip $3.50, cortado $4.25, latte $5.25, pourover $6.00, cold brew $5.50, 12oz House Blend Ember $18, 12oz Single Origin Ethiopia Guji $22. Principles we hold to: Raise prices annually by a small amount rather than rarely by a large one. A 4% increase produced no measurable complaint; the 11% jump in year two produced three weeks of them in Customer Feedback Log. Never discount the coffee. Reward frequency instead through Loyalty Program, and never lead an email with a promotion, per Email Newsletter Strategy. Price single origins to their true cost including shrinkage from the Roasting Schedule, not to match the blend. Wholesale pricing is a separate ladder based on volume and delivery cost, held in Wholesale Accounts. Every price change is modelled against Cost of Goods Breakdown with a 32% ceiling on goods, and the impact lands in Monthly PnL Summary within two months. When green coffee costs jump, per Green Bean Inventory, we absorb one season and then reprice. We do not shrink the bag. Related: Seasonal Menu Autumn, Quarterly OKRs

notes.label: Email Newsletter Strategy
notes.excerpt: One email every two weeks, Thursday 9am, plain text with one photo. 2,900 subscribers, 41% open rate, 4% click rate. The list comes almost entirely from Loyalty Program signups. Structure that earns the open: One paragraph of something true and specific — a lot arriving, a batch that surprised us, a staffing change. One thing to buy, with a link. Usually the current Single Origin Ethiopia Guji or a subscription. One thing happening — a cupping, a menu change from Seasonal Menu Autumn, the Farmers Market Booth schedule. Email drives subscriptions better than any other channel. It also saves them: the win-back sequence described in Subscription Churn Notes runs from this list and recovers…

The best performing email we have ever sent was an apology for running out of a lot from Green Bean Inventory. Related: Regulars and Community, Local Press Outreach

notes.text: Saturday market on Hawthorne, 8am to 1pm, April through October. Two staff, a folding table, a grinder, a hand-pour setup, and about 60 bags of coffee. Direct economics are mediocre. Average market Saturday grosses $780 with roughly $310 of staff and stall cost against it. As a sales channel it barely clears the bar set in Monthly PnL Summary. As an acquisition channel it is the best thing we do. Roughly 30 loyalty signups per market, tracked with a market-specific code from Loyalty Program, and those signups retain better than Instagram signups because they have already tasted the coffee and met a human. What sells: 12oz bags of House Blend Ember to people who have never heard of us, and Single Origin Ethiopia Guji to the ones who ask a second question. Brewed samples in small cups are non-negotiable — no samples, half the sales. Bring the cupping notes and let people taste two coffees side by side. That conversation is the same one that works on the pourover flight in Seasonal Menu Autumn. Staffing comes out of the Saturday roster and must not thin the café bar during its own rush — the constraint written into Staff Scheduling Rules. It is also where two of our three Wholesale Accounts first found us, and where the reporter behind Local Press Outreach first tried the coffee. Related: Instagram Content Plan, Second Location Analysis

notes.label: Instagram Content Plan
notes.excerpt: Instagram is our only real acquisition channel and it works because it looks like a coffee bar, not an ad agency. Four posts a week, shot on a phone, natural light only, no stock imagery ever. The rotation: Monday: process. Roasting, cupping, a scale, hands. The Roasting Schedule is quietly the best content generator we have. Wednesday: people. A barista, a regular, the Ivy Street baker from Pastry Partnership. Faces outperform latte art by roughly three to one on saves. Friday: product. Whatever just came off the roaster, usually Single Origin Ethiopia Guji or a bag of House Blend Ember. Sunday: place. The room, the light at 7am, the queue. Stories daily, unpolished, with the menu board…

New follower to first purchase is roughly 6%, tracked through codes in Loyalty Program. Related: Local Press Outreach, Farmers Market Booth

notes.text: Three pieces of coverage in three years, all of them from relationships rather than pitches. What worked. A food writer for the weekly tried our coffee at the Farmers Market Booth, asked about the sourcing behind Single Origin Ethiopia Guji, and wrote 800 words about traceability. That piece produced a two-week traffic spike and, more usefully, two of our current Wholesale Accounts. What did not work. A press release. A paid listicle placement. A paid influencer visit that produced one story and no measurable visits, an experiment we will not repeat and which is noted against the marketing line in Monthly PnL Summary. The angle that gets written about is always specific and slightly awkward: we do not bake our own pastry and we say why, per Pastry Partnership. We tell people when a lot runs out instead of substituting it, per Green Bean Inventory. We only roast twice a week, per Roasting Schedule. Specificity is the story. Standing practice: when a journalist walks in, they get a seat, a taste, and twenty minutes, no matter how busy the bar is. Shift leads know to page the owner — the exception written into Staff Scheduling Rules. Coverage gets amplified once through Instagram Content Plan and once in Email Newsletter Strategy, then left alone. Related: Competitor Landscape, Regulars and Community

notes.label: Loyalty Program
notes.excerpt: Digital card in the point of sale, no app to download. Ten drinks earns one free drink of equal or lesser value. 1,340 active members, defined as at least one visit in 60 days. What the data says. Members visit 2.4 times a week against 1.3 for non-members and spend 22% more per ticket, mostly because they attach a pastry from Pastry Partnership. The free drink costs us about $0.71 in goods, which is trivial against the visit frequency it buys — the arithmetic is in Cost of Goods Breakdown. Bonus mechanics we actually use: Double points before 7:30am, to thicken the early rush described in Daily Opening Checklist. Bonus points for trying two new drinks at a menu launch, per Seasonal Menu…

notes.excerpt: The La Marzocco Linea PB is a three-group machine bought used in year one, financed under the terms in Equipment Loan Terms. It is the most expensive thing in the building and the fastest way to lose a day of trade. Daily, closing shift: backflush every group with water, then with detergent, brush the group heads, soak baskets and portafilters, wipe steam wands and purge them. Grinder hopper emptied and wiped Sunday. Weekly: descale check on the water softener, drain tray deep clean, replace the shower screens if they are pitted, calibrate the grinder against a scale rather than by feel. notes.text: The La Marzocco Linea PB is a three-group machine bought used in year one, financed under the terms in Equipment Loan Terms. It is the most expensive thing in the building and the fastest way to lose a day of trade. Daily, closing shift: backflush every group with water, then with detergent, brush the group heads, soak baskets and portafilters, wipe steam wands and purge them. Grinder hopper emptied and wiped Sunday. Weekly: descale check on the water softener, drain tray deep clean, replace the shower screens if they are pitted, calibrate the grinder against a scale rather than by feel. Quarterly: technician visit. Gaskets, valves, pressure calibration, water filter cartridge. Book it, do not wait for a symptom. Symptoms and what they usually mean: Shots running fast and sour with no grind change: worn burrs or stale beans, cross-check the Roasting Schedule batch date. Group leaking at the edge: gasket, not technique. Steam pressure dropping mid-rush: descale overdue. Every barista learns this list in week one of the Barista Training Plan. Downtime costs roughly $900 in lost daily revenue against the numbers in Monthly PnL Summary, which is more than any service visit. Related: Daily Opening Checklist, Staff Scheduling Rules

notes.text: Green coffee is our single largest asset and the easiest thing to quietly waste. Count it every Monday morning before the week's plan is set. Current standing lots: Ethiopia Guji, washed, 6 bags (60kg each) — the star of Single Origin Ethiopia Guji. Fast mover, reorder at 3 bags. Colombia Huila, 9 bags — the base of House Blend Ember. Reorder at 5 bags. Brazil Cerrado natural, 7 bags — blend body and the cold brew base. Reorder at 4 bags. Sumatra Mandheling, 2 bags — winter only, do not reorder until October. Swiss Water decaf, 3 bags — wholesale demand only. Storage: pallets off the floor, 60-70°F, under 60% humidity, away from the roaster exhaust wall. Green coffee holds well for about nine months from harvest arrival, after which it tastes flat and papery no matter how well we roast it. Two failure modes have actually cost us money. First, over-buying a seasonal lot we could not sell before it faded. Second, running out of Colombia mid-week and improvising the blend, which produced two weeks of customer complaints logged in Customer Feedback Log. Orders go through the vetted list in Supplier Directory, and every purchase order gets matched to the value shown in Monthly PnL Summary. Related: Roasting Schedule, Pricing Strategy

notes.label: Roasting Schedule
notes.excerpt: We roast Tuesday and Friday on the 12kg Loring. Two roast days keeps everything the café pulls within a 4-11 day window off roast, which is where our blends taste best. Tuesday is wholesale day. Batches run in this order: House Blend Ember (four batches, 9kg green each), then the decaf, then whatever wholesale single origin is on contract. Bags are labelled, one-way valved, and staged for the Wednesday delivery run described in Wholesale Accounts. Friday is retail and subscription day. Single Origin Ethiopia Guji runs first while the drum is cleanest, then House Blend Ember for the retail shelf, then sample roasts for whatever we are evaluating from the Supplier Directory. Rules we do not break: Log every batch: green weight, charge temp, first crack time, drop temp, end weight, shrinkage. Target shrinkage is 14-16%. Never roast a lot without cupping the previous roast of it first. Green stock check before you build the day's plan — see Green Bean Inventory. If a lot is under 20kg, flag it for reorder, not for a bigger batch. Roast profiles live in the shared sheet, not in someone's head. Shrinkage and batch loss feed straight into Cost of Goods Breakdown, so sloppy logging shows up as fake margin. Related: Quarterly OKRs, Seasonal Menu Autumn

Pay moves at sign-off under Payroll and Tips Policy, and the roster in Staff Scheduling Rules assumes trained staff on every shift. Related: Hiring Pipeline, Cold Brew Recipe

notes.excerpt: We hire about four people a year to hold a team of nine. Two are replacements, which is a turnover rate we would like to halve. Process, four steps. What we look for, in order: warmth with strangers, composure under a queue, willingness to be corrected, and only then coffee experience. Referrals from current staff, which produce the best retention and are worth a bonus under Payroll and Tips Policy. Regulars who ask, per Regulars and Community. A sign in the window. Never a job board, which produced twelve applications and no hires. Timing. Hire before the summer cold brew season in Cold Brew Recipe and before an autumn launch in Seasonal Menu Autumn, because a four week ramp means a September hire is useless in September. The roster constraints in Staff Scheduling Rules set the real deadline. A roaster hire is a different search entirely and would be the first requirement of either Second Location Analysis or the wholesale growth in Wholesale Accounts. Related: Quarterly OKRs, Monthly PnL Summary

Referral bonus of $200 after a new hire's ninetieth day, which is the cheapest recruiting channel we have, per Hiring Pipeline. The economics. Labour at 37% of revenue in Monthly PnL Summary looks high against industry benchmarks. Replacing a barista costs about $2,400 in training time and lost speed, and customers name staff in almost all the praise recorded in Customer Feedback Log. Paying above market is cheaper than churning, and the regulars in Regulars and Community are attached to faces. Any wage change is modelled before a price change, not after, per Pricing Strategy. Related: Quarterly OKRs, Second Location Analysis

notes.label: Staff Scheduling Rules
notes.excerpt: Labour is 37% of revenue in Monthly PnL Summary and it is the number that decides whether a month is good. It is also the number that, cut wrongly, destroys the thing customers actually pay for. Hard rules Two on bar from 7 to 10 on weekdays. The rush between 7:10 and 8:45 in Daily Opening Checklist is 40% of weekday transactions and one person cannot hold it. Opening shift is always someone signed off under Barista Training Plan, never a trainee alone. The Farmers Market Booth Saturday crew is additional headcount, never pulled off the café bar. Roast days are protected. Tuesday and Friday mornings the roaster is not also on bar, per Roasting Schedule. Schedule published 10 days out…

Soft patterns that work: 2pm to close is one person plus prep; Mondays are thin and the right day for deep cleaning under Espresso Machine Maintenance; the pastry order in Pastry Partnership is set by the shift lead who saw the traffic. Understaffing shows up within two weeks as slow service complaints in Customer Feedback Log and as turnover, which is far more expensive than the shift we saved — the argument in Payroll and Tips Policy. Related: Hiring Pipeline, Quarterly OKRs

notes.label: Cold Brew Recipe
notes.excerpt: Cold brew is 18% of summer revenue and nearly zero labour once the batch is built, which makes it the best margin item on the menu. Concentrate recipe: 1kg coarse ground Brazil Cerrado to 8 litres cold filtered water. Steep 18 hours at cellar temperature, never in the walk-in — cold steeping under 50°F strips the sweetness. Filter through the cloth sock, then a paper polish. Yield is about 7 litres of concentrate. Service: cut 1:1 with water over ice for the tap pour, 1:1.5 for the canned wholesale format. Nitro tap runs at 32 psi on beer gas. Keg lasts three days in summer, five in winter, and gets dumped at day six regardless. Use the Brazil, not the blend. We tested House Blend Ember in…
notes.text: Cold brew is 18% of summer revenue and nearly zero labour once the batch is built, which makes it the best margin item on the menu. Concentrate recipe: 1kg coarse ground Brazil Cerrado to 8 litres cold filtered water. Steep 18 hours at cellar temperature, never in the walk-in — cold steeping under 50°F strips the sweetness. Filter through the cloth sock, then a paper polish. Yield is about 7 litres of concentrate. Service: cut 1:1 with water over ice for the tap pour, 1:1.5 for the canned wholesale format. Nitro tap runs at 32 psi on beer gas. Keg lasts three days in summer, five in winter, and gets dumped at day six regardless. Use the Brazil, not the blend. We tested House Blend Ember in cold brew and the Ethiopian component turned sour by hour twelve. Green stock for this comes off the Brazil line in Green Bean Inventory. Batch cadence sits on the Roasting Schedule as coarse grind Thursday, and the tap check is step five of the Daily Opening Checklist. Margin detail is worked out in Cost of Goods Breakdown: roughly 82% gross on the tap pour, our single best number, which is why the canned version is a candidate for Wholesale Accounts expansion. Related: Seasonal Menu Autumn, Pricing Strategy

notes.excerpt: Our signature blend and about 55% of everything we roast. If a customer only ever buys one bag from us, it is this one. Tastes like milk chocolate, toasted almond, dried cherry on the finish. Built to hold up in milk without disappearing. notes.text: Our signature blend and about 55% of everything we roast. If a customer only ever buys one bag from us, it is this one. Recipe: 60% Colombia Huila (washed), 30% Brazil Cerrado (natural), 10% Ethiopia Guji (washed). Medium roast, dropped at 410°F, 16% shrinkage. Tastes like milk chocolate, toasted almond, dried cherry on the finish. Built to hold up in milk without disappearing. Why it works commercially: the Colombia and Brazil are volume lots with stable pricing from Supplier Directory, so the blend cost stays predictable even when specialty prices spike. The 10% Ethiopia is the aroma and the story — it is also the component most at risk when the lot in Green Bean Inventory runs low. It is the espresso in every milk drink, the wholesale default in Wholesale Accounts, the anchor of the 12oz retail bag, and the default in the subscription discussed in Subscription Churn Notes. Rest window: four to twelve days off roast, per the Roasting Schedule. Under four days it gasses out and channels; past two weeks it goes flat and the cherry note vanishes. Do not reformulate this quietly. Two changes in three years, both cupped blind against the old recipe and both announced to wholesale partners first. Related: Pricing Strategy, Cost of Goods Breakdown, Barista Training Plan

notes.label: Pastry Partnership
notes.excerpt: We do not bake. We tried for four months in year two and it cost us a staff member and a lot of goodwill. Ivy Street Bakery, three blocks away, now supplies everything in the case. Terms: we buy wholesale at 45% of our retail price, delivered daily at 6:05am, and we carry the waste. Order is placed the previous day by 2pm based on the shift lead's read of the week. Standing order is 24 croissants, 12 almond, 18 morning buns, 10 gluten free, plus a rotating tart. Waste is the whole game. Above 8% waste and the category stops making money. We hit 11% in the first quarter of the deal because we ordered for the weekend we wanted, not the Tuesday we had. Now the order follows the traffic pattern recorded in Staff Scheduling Rules and the numbers land in Cost of Goods Breakdown. Counting the delivery against the invoice is step six of the Daily Opening Checklist. Shorted items happen about twice a month and Ivy Street credits them without argument. Pastry pulls average ticket from $6.10 to $9.40 when it attaches, which is the most valuable single fact in Monthly PnL Summary. Baristas are trained to offer it, never to push it — see Barista Training Plan. Related: Supplier Directory, Regulars and Community, Pricing Strategy

When it runs out we do not fake it with another Ethiopian, we tell people, which is the practice defended in Local Press Outreach. It is the coffee that gets written about, features in most of the Instagram Content Plan posts, and pulls new subscribers more than anything else we sell. It also contributes 10% of House Blend Ember. Related: Green Bean Inventory, Pricing Strategy, Seasonal Menu Autumn

The most respected roaster in the city, more expensive than us, wholesale-first, minimal café. A regional chain, cheaper by about 15%, faster, open at 5:30am, and consistently mediocre. They win the pure commuter who wants speed. We do not compete on speed; we compete on the 8am customer who will wait four minutes, per Regulars and Community. Fathom Roasters (half a mile). The most respected roaster in the city, more expensive than us, wholesale-first, minimal café. They are the reason we sit second on price rather than first, per Pricing Strategy, and they are the real competition for the accounts in Wholesale Accounts. The Hartwell Hotel café. Not a competitor — a customer. They buy 9kg a week from us. Kiosk on Hawthorne. Seasonal, cash only, competes with the Farmers Market Booth on Saturdays and beats us on convenience, never on coffee. Where we actually win: staff continuity, traceable sourcing like Single Origin Ethiopia Guji, the pastry case from Pastry Partnership, and being the shop people bring visitors to. That last one is the story in Local Press Outreach. Where we lose: price against Bluewater, roasting reputation against Fathom, hours against everyone. Hours are the cheapest of those to fix and would need the headcount in Hiring Pipeline. Related: Second Location Analysis, Quarterly OKRs, Monthly PnL Summary

notes.text: Three objectives, no more. Anything not on this page is maintenance. Objective 1 — make wholesale the stable half of the business. Grow Wholesale Accounts from $12,600 to $16,000 a month. Land two accounts, at least one from the canned product in Cold Brew Recipe. Zero consistency incidents, meaning zero improvised blends of House Blend Ember during a stockout, which requires the reorder discipline in Green Bean Inventory. Objective 2 — stop leaking subscribers. Cut monthly churn from 6.5% to 4.5%, per Subscription Churn Notes. Offer a cadence change at every cancellation. Put a rotating single origin, usually Single Origin Ethiopia Guji, in front of every subscriber past their third shipment via Email Newsletter Strategy. Objective 3 — hold margin without raising prices twice. Labour to 35% of revenue in Monthly PnL Summary through the roster discipline in Staff Scheduling Rules, without cutting the two-on-bar rule. Pastry waste under 8%, per Pastry Partnership. Cost of goods under 30%, per Cost of Goods Breakdown. Explicitly not this quarter: a second site. The trigger conditions live in Second Location Analysis and none of them are met. Reviewed the first Monday of the quarter against Pricing Strategy and Hiring Pipeline. Related: Competitor Landscape, Payroll and Tips Policy

notes.label: Second Location Analysis
notes.excerpt: The question we keep circling. Honest answer today: not yet, and here is what would change it. The case for. The Loring has headroom — about 96kg of green a week across two roast days per Equipment Loan Terms — so a second café would be supplied by an asset we already own. Brand awareness from Instagram Content Plan and Local Press Outreach extends past the neighbourhood we actually trade in. The case against, in order of seriousness. People. A second bar needs a shift lead we do not have and a hiring pipeline running at roughly double its current rate, per Hiring Pipeline and Barista Training Plan. Cash. Net is about $6,000 a month in Monthly PnL Summary. Build-out is $180,000 to $240,000…

The Loring has headroom — about 96kg of green a week across two roast days per Equipment Loan Terms — so a second café would be supplied by an asset we already own. Brand awareness from Instagram Content Plan and Local Press Outreach extends past the neighbourhood we actually trade in. The case against, in order of seriousness. People. A second bar needs a shift lead we do not have and a hiring pipeline running at roughly double its current rate, per Hiring Pipeline and Barista Training Plan. Cash. Net is about $6,000 a month in Monthly PnL Summary. Build-out is $180,000 to $240,000 and both existing notes are personally guaranteed. The thing that makes this shop work is not replicable. Trigger conditions: two consecutive quarters of net above $9,000, a trained shift lead in place, and wholesale above $18,000 a month. Tracked in Quarterly OKRs.
